Static analysis · ELF64 x86-64 static executable (stripped, no interpreter) · 2026-10-22

Mirai botnet

MaliciousRole: payloadCapability: botnetFamily: Mirai · confidence 0.55

A stripped, static x86-64 Linux executable with no imports (E21): an unpacked Mirai-derived DDoS bot with an added backdoor shell. Its strings sit in a 476-slot table ChaCha20-decrypted at start-up, with the cipher constant masked (B1). On a victim host it runs as one daemonised instance under a random process name. As root it hides its pid behind another process's /proc entry and kills competing processes (B3-B5). It registers with its C2 over an X25519-keyed, ChaCha20/HMAC channel (B6, B7). For its operator it is a flood node with 24 attack vectors (B8), an interactive shell on the host (B10, B11) and a self-update path (B9).

How it runs

The behaviours as a flow, from the entry point: the checks that can end the run, then what it collects, then what it sends and what follows. Boxes follow the order of the analyst's account; a dashed box is code whose path from the entry is not proven. Static analysis: not an observed run.

Throughout: Encrypted string store (B1); Daemonises and masquerades (B3).

What it does in the full report →

main decrypts the store first. 461 entries come out: identifiers, paths, 24 hostnames and format strings (B1; E22, E24, E34, E35-E37). A listener on loopback port I2 enforces a single instance, and a newer copy that connects to it takes over (B2; E9). A one-byte marker page is mapped read-only from a file, a /proc-found mapping or a memfd (E33; U5).

The bot then forks, calls setsid and closes stdio. As root it sets itself non-dumpable and takes a store name through prctl and argv[0] (B3; E11). It bind-mounts a donor process's /proc directory over its own (B4; E12). Workers walk /proc and kill processes whose names match store identifiers (B5; E19, E25).

The C2 host is store slots 0-7, I3 (E24, E29). Resolution tries a literal address, then getaddrinfo, then the bot's own DNS queries to 18 embedded public resolvers (E17, E18). The port is random from a 14-entry table, I20-I33 (E30). The hello carries a fresh X25519 key against a peer key derived from 32 embedded bytes, and encrypts the registration record: CPU count, memory, uname, euid and limits (B6, B7; E14, E31). Incoming frames are tag-checked and then ChaCha20-decrypted, or XORed with one byte in a plain mode (E15, E32; U2).

Attack commands follow Mirai's layout: duration, vector id, IP/prefix targets and options (E6). A forked worker calls the vector from a 24-entry {id, function} table, and a sibling ends it after the duration (B8; E7, E8; U4). Command 0xff kills the bot's children. Command 0xfe downloads from I13, sets the file to 0755 and executes it (B9; E13).

A second message class opens a pty shell (B11; E26, E28). The slave becomes the child's controlling terminal and stdio, and the child executes a store shell path. Its user and home values come from store-named programs, run through a pipe/fork/execve runner, and from the account entry matching getuid (B10; E27). Output is relayed back over the C2, with a pipe fallback.

Not recovered: 23 store entries and the other hostname slots' readers (U1), the embedded key bytes and primitives (U2), the shell relay (U3), vector templates (U4) and the marker page's reader (U5).

Verdict and detection opportunities all anchor details →

Malicious botnet payload with backdoor capability. The family is Mirai at 0.55: there is no corpus label, and the code follows Mirai's source structure throughout (E1, E6, E7, E9, E10). The decoded strings name no variant.

  • A1: the masked ChaCha20 constant is a fixed 16-byte run, confirmed against RFC 7539 (E37).
  • A2: the 24-record method table is the lineage's dispatch structure (E7, E8).
  • A3: the /proc bind-mount routine survives store re-keying (E12).
  • A4: the resolver table is build-specific (E17, E18).
  • A5: the loopback lock constants are weak alone (E9).

Open questions in the full report →

  1. 23 of 484 string-store sites fail the printable control, and the readers of the other hostname-class slots (0x8-0x10, 0x114, 0x13f-0x143) are not known.
    Why it stopped: the 23 sites fail the printable-likeness control (short entries, likely binary values or a second scheme); no xref pass for slots 0x8-0x10 and 0x13f-0x143 was run
  2. Where the 32 bytes behind the C2 peer key live, and the exact hash/MAC primitives of the session.
    Why it stopped: 0x4122e0 (source of the embedded bytes), 0x411241 (hash) and 0x412677 (MAC) were not opened; the capa HMAC/Curve25519 leads agree with the read but the primitives are not named by a read
  3. The shell relay 0x40a31c and the shell-message check 0x40b0b8.
    Why it stopped: the relay and the magic check were not opened; the shell itself is established
  4. Protocol and packet template of each of the 24 attack vectors at 0x62b000.
    Why it stopped: vector bodies not read individually; a per-vector read matters for network signatures only
  5. What the read-only marker page at 0x62bdc0 is used for after 0x40c8fe maps it.
    Why it stopped: the readers of 0x62bdc0 were not followed
  6. Reach of 9 user functions (among them 0x401a5e and 0x4021f5, which connect and send) and 28 unresolved computed sites in reached code.
    Why it stopped: native_callgraph.py and dispatch_reach.py parse PE only (PEFormatError on this ELF); no ELF code-slot pass was run

Summary

A stripped, static x86-64 Linux executable with no imports (E21): an unpacked Mirai-derived DDoS bot with an added backdoor shell. Its strings sit in a 476-slot table ChaCha20-decrypted at start-up, with the cipher constant masked (B1). On a victim host it runs as one daemonised instance under a random process name. As root it hides its pid behind another process's /proc entry and kills competing processes (B3-B5). It registers with its C2 over an X25519-keyed, ChaCha20/HMAC channel (B6, B7). For its operator it is a flood node with 24 attack vectors (B8), an interactive shell on the host (B10, B11) and a self-update path (B9).

Behaviour

main decrypts the store first. 461 entries come out: identifiers, paths, 24 hostnames and format strings (B1; E22, E24, E34, E35-E37). A listener on loopback port I2 enforces a single instance, and a newer copy that connects to it takes over (B2; E9). A one-byte marker page is mapped read-only from a file, a /proc-found mapping or a memfd (E33; U5).

The bot then forks, calls setsid and closes stdio. As root it sets itself non-dumpable and takes a store name through prctl and argv[0] (B3; E11). It bind-mounts a donor process's /proc directory over its own (B4; E12). Workers walk /proc and kill processes whose names match store identifiers (B5; E19, E25).

The C2 host is store slots 0-7, I3 (E24, E29). Resolution tries a literal address, then getaddrinfo, then the bot's own DNS queries to 18 embedded public resolvers (E17, E18). The port is random from a 14-entry table, I20-I33 (E30). The hello carries a fresh X25519 key against a peer key derived from 32 embedded bytes, and encrypts the registration record: CPU count, memory, uname, euid and limits (B6, B7; E14, E31). Incoming frames are tag-checked and then ChaCha20-decrypted, or XORed with one byte in a plain mode (E15, E32; U2).

Attack commands follow Mirai's layout: duration, vector id, IP/prefix targets and options (E6). A forked worker calls the vector from a 24-entry {id, function} table, and a sibling ends it after the duration (B8; E7, E8; U4). Command 0xff kills the bot's children. Command 0xfe downloads from I13, sets the file to 0755 and executes it (B9; E13).

A second message class opens a pty shell (B11; E26, E28). The slave becomes the child's controlling terminal and stdio, and the child executes a store shell path. Its user and home values come from store-named programs, run through a pipe/fork/execve runner, and from the account entry matching getuid (B10; E27). Output is relayed back over the C2, with a pipe fallback.

Not recovered: 23 store entries and the other hostname slots' readers (U1), the embedded key bytes and primitives (U2), the shell relay (U3), vector templates (U4) and the marker page's reader (U5).

Verdict and anchors

Malicious botnet payload with backdoor capability. The family is Mirai at 0.55: there is no corpus label, and the code follows Mirai's source structure throughout (E1, E6, E7, E9, E10). The decoded strings name no variant.

  • A1: the masked ChaCha20 constant is a fixed 16-byte run, confirmed against RFC 7539 (E37).
  • A2: the 24-record method table is the lineage's dispatch structure (E7, E8).
  • A3: the /proc bind-mount routine survives store re-keying (E12).
  • A4: the resolver table is build-specific (E17, E18).
  • A5: the loopback lock constants are weak alone (E9).

Original file, unpacked file
The original file is the sample as collected. An unpacked file is one the analysis extracted or decoded from it, numbered in order (in report.json: L0, L1, L2…).
Reachable from the entry point
The static call graph shows a path from where the program starts to this code. It does not mean the code was seen running.
Code present, path not proven
The code is in the file, but the analysis could not prove a route to it, usually because of indirect calls or jump tables.
B, E, A, U, D numbers
Behaviours, evidence items, detection anchors, open questions (unknowns) and derived files (such as decoded strings). Every claim cites the evidence items it rests on.
API hashing
Looking up Windows functions at run time by a hash of their name, so the names never appear in the file.
MBA
Mixed boolean-arithmetic: computing a simple constant through a tangle of AND, OR, XOR and arithmetic.
ATT&CK, MBC
Public catalogues of attacker techniques (MITRE ATT&CK) and malware behaviours (MBC).
IOC
Indicator of compromise: a value, such as a domain or file name, that shows up on an infected host or network.

why
No corpus family label (cluster elf/unk). Code structure matches the Mirai source: main loop with loopback single-instance lock and takeover, local address via UDP connect to a public resolver on port 53, attack_parse layout (u32 duration, u8 vector, ip+prefix targets, length-prefixed options), forked attack workers dispatched from an {id, fn} method table, slot-id string table. A heavily extended derivative: ChaCha20 string store (461 of 484 entries recovered, E35), 24 vectors, X25519-keyed ChaCha20/HMAC C2 session, a remote PTY shell (backdoor capability beside the DDoS bot), /proc bind-mount hiding. The decoded strings name no variant, so the variant stays unnamed.

Open questions 6

Questions the analysis could not answer, what was tried, and why it stopped. Some may have been answered by a later step; check Decoded strings.

U1

23 of 484 string-store sites fail the printable control, and the readers of the other hostname-class slots (0x8-0x10, 0x114, 0x13f-0x143) are not known.

what was tried
ChaCha20 decrypt of all 484 setter sites (E35, E36, E37): 461 accepted under the printable control, 3 wrong-parameter variants accept none, slot-to-class map for the analysed readers (E25, E34), read the C2 selector 0x413189 and port picker 0x413aaa (E29, E30): the C2 host is slots 0-7 and the port comes from the 0x4287e0 table
why it stopped
the 23 sites fail the printable-likeness control (short entries, likely binary values or a second scheme); no xref pass for slots 0x8-0x10 and 0x13f-0x143 was run
blocks
none
evidence
E35, E36, E29
U2

Where the 32 bytes behind the C2 peer key live, and the exact hash/MAC primitives of the session.

what was tried
read the handshake 0x411a32, the peer-key derivation 0x411361 and the frame receive 0x412ad8/0x412010 (E31, E32): X25519 ephemeral key, peer key = clamp(hash(32 embedded bytes)), key expansion with a store label, 16-byte tag then ChaCha20
why it stopped
0x4122e0 (source of the embedded bytes), 0x411241 (hash) and 0x412677 (MAC) were not opened; the capa HMAC/Curve25519 leads agree with the read but the primitives are not named by a read
blocks
none
evidence
E31, E32, E16
U3

The shell relay 0x40a31c and the shell-message check 0x40b0b8.

what was tried
read 0x40aa12 in full (E26), the frame parser 0x40b0fb (E28) and the environment discovery 0x40a57f/0x40a86a (E27): the second command class is a remote PTY shell
why it stopped
the relay and the magic check were not opened; the shell itself is established
blocks
none
U4

Protocol and packet template of each of the 24 attack vectors at 0x62b000.

what was tried
table dumped (out/L0/method_table.json); syscall profile per vector (out/L0/fn_syscalls.json)
why it stopped
vector bodies not read individually; a per-vector read matters for network signatures only
blocks
none
U5

What the read-only marker page at 0x62bdc0 is used for after 0x40c8fe maps it.

what was tried
read 0x40c8fe, 0x40c6f4 and 0x40c63d (E33): one byte written to an existing file, a /proc-found mapping, a memfd or a 0600 file, then mapped PROT_READ; no copy of the binary is written, so it is not a persistence drop
why it stopped
the readers of 0x62bdc0 were not followed
blocks
none
U6

Reach of 9 user functions (among them 0x401a5e and 0x4021f5, which connect and send) and 28 unresolved computed sites in reached code.

what was tried
Ghidra call graph plus the 24 attack-table slots as roots
why it stopped
native_callgraph.py and dispatch_reach.py parse PE only (PEFormatError on this ELF); no ELF code-slot pass was run
blocks
none
